newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Ruggiero hopes for common ground on labour standard.
newsitem.headline: Ruggiero hopes for common ground on labour standard.

text.p: World Trade Organisation (WTO) director-general Renato Ruggiero expressed confidence on Sunday that this week's meeting of WTO ministers would establish common ground on the controversial issue of labour standards.

Speaking to trade unionists on the eve of the opening of the WTO ministerial meeting in Singapore, Ruggiero said he believed a paragraph could be agreed for inclusion in the closing declaration if all participating ministers showed flexibility.
"The disagreements are not as huge as they were," Ruggiero said.
He said he was proud of the progress that had been made towards a consensus over the basis for discussing the link between trade and core labour standards.
"We are in a situation where no one contests that there could be common ground in our discussion," Ruggiero said.

The United States, with the backing of some European countries, wants the contentious issue of labour standards placed on the global trade agenda in a bid to win WTO recognition of basic workers' rights.
Asian countries, including India, Pakistan and Malaysia, are fiercely opposed to a move which they say smacks of protectionism.
Ruggiero said he was also confident that agreement could be reached in three other tricky areas -- textiles, agriculture and the future work programme of the WTO.
He said each subject was politically very sensitive but that negotiators had made considerable progress during preparatory discussions at WTO headquarters in Geneva.
"I hope the common ground we have covered in Geneva will not be lost," Ruggiero said.
The director-general said differences separating ministers in the area of liberalisation of information technology were big but bridgeable.
He stressed the importance of reaching an agreement, saying new information technologies were as important for the world economy as water.
"If you do not have water you cannot survive," Ruggiero said.
Ministers from the world trade body's 125 member states open a five-day meeting on Monday. REUTER
